title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a widely used data-free method for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) using machine learning. With recent advances in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), adversarial learning has shown strong capabilities for modeling complex data-driven problems; however, the use of GANs in deterministic physics-informed PDE solutions remains limited. In this work, we first identify limitations of standard PINNs for solving PDEs, including spectral bias, loss imbalance, and optimizer stagnation. We then propose Generative Adversarial Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Gen-PINNs), a unified deterministic residual-adversarial framework designed to improve data-free solutions of PDEs with sharp or shock-front behavior. The generator learns the underlying PDE solution using dynamically weighted physics-informed loss components, while separate discriminators evaluate complementary PDE residual features against ideal zero-residual states. The framework further develops and adapts several methodological components, including a Fourier representation for resolving high-frequency spatial content, an orthonormal spectral diagnostic for quantifying frequency-dependent solution errors, and a modified gradient-based dynamic weighting system for physics, initial-condition, boundary-condition, and adversarial loss objectives. Gen-PINNs is tested against standard PINNs on nonlinear and higher-order PDEs, including the Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and convergence across sharp-front, stiff, and higher-order PDE solutions, highlighting the potential of deterministic residual-adversarial learning as an effective approach for solving challenging nonlinear PDEs.

title: Overcoming the limitations of body-ordered potentials for atomistic machine learning
abstract: Machine-learning interatomic potentials have become indispensable tools in atomistic simulations. The most popular models rely heavily on physical priors, such as locality, smoothness and symmetry, that are assumed to improve the accuracy and transferability of the trained models. However, recent evidence suggests that, in the data-rich regime, unconstrained models that learn symmetry from the data can achieve very competitive accuracy and computational efficiency, without sacrificing stability and generalization power. Many equivariant symmetric architectures historically rely on the assumption that the interatomic potential can be approximated well by a convergentcluster expansion, i.e., a decomposition in terms associated to atomic pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and higher-order tuples. We describe an architecture that incorporates locality, smoothness, and symmetry priors, but that -- thanks to a computationally efficient tensor product formulation -- does not assume low-order truncation of the body-ordered series.

title: Sequential Random Sampling PIR with Multiple Colluding Servers in DNA-Based Data Storage
abstract: As DNA-based data storage evolves, protecting user privacy during data retrieval has become increasingly important. We study sequential random sampling DNA private information retrieval (SRS DNA PIR) with multiple colluding random sampling servers, where the database is partitioned into servers of equal size. We investigate the tradeoff between the download cost, defined as the expected number of queries, and the privacy leakage, measured by mutual information. We derive lower bounds on this tradeoff, including a bound given by an optimization problem. This bound is tight when each server stores two files, and we construct schemes that attain it. For servers of any size, we construct schemes that apply a single-server scheme to a randomly selected subset of servers.

title: Learning Traffic Flow Dynamics with Stochastic Physics-Informed Neural Cellular Automata
abstract: Traffic flow modeling is essential for understanding and predicting the collective dynamics of vehicles on road networks. Cellular automata provide a simple, interpretable yet powerful framework for representing these dynamics via local interaction rules, while retaining the ability to reproduce complex macroscopic traffic phenomena. However, learning local transition rules from data while preserving physically meaningful constraints remains challenging, particularly for stochastic models. In this work, we propose a physics-informed neural cellular automaton (PI-NCA) for data-driven traffic flow modeling. title: Adjoint-Based Calibration and Optimal Control of Stochastic Multiscale Bioprocess Digital Twins
abstract: We develop a bias-aware digital-twin calibration and control framework for multiscale bioprocess models within a biological systems-of-systems (Bio-SoS) paradigm. The digital twin is represented by a stochastic differential equation (SDE) model and calibrated from sparse, discrete observations using quasi-likelihood estimation and adjoint sensitivity analysis. SDE generator-based moment expansions characterize truncation-induced parameter bias, while forward-backward adjoints quantify how calibration uncertainty propagates to value functions and policy performance. The resulting parameter-error distribution supports both policy-directed adaptive experimental design and uncertainty-aware policy optimization through a second-order Gaussian-averaged objective. We characterize the asymptotic behavior of the resulting exploration criterion and derive a physical-system performance under the optimized policy. To implement these ideas, we develop an Actor-Simulator algorithm that jointly updates model parameters, selects informative experiments, and optimizes control policies. Numerical studies demonstrate improved calibration accuracy, sample efficiency, and control performance relative to state-of-the-art baselines.

title: An Executable Lie Lattice Compiler (Lean 4, Finsupp) with Exact Provenance Recovery
abstract: Perfect Provenance in High-Dimensional Lattices Abstract In high-dimensional lattice calculations—such as quantum mechanics or multi-dimensional transport simulation—explicit matrix tracking collapses due to the curse of dimensionality. Furthermore, standard algebraic simplifications like A + B - A \Rightarrow B create a catastrophic loss of history, completely obliterating information provenance. We introduce a novel, fully verified computational architecture in Lean 4 that models multidimensional integer-linear transport operators (u^\alpha \partial_i) and tracks their algebraic lineage without a single sorry axiom. By imposing explicit discrete topologies (\tau = \bot), we construct rigid topological homeomorphisms (bracketHomeomorph and graphHomeomorph) between syntactic expression trees and active evaluation states. This structural decoupling guarantees that exact metadata addresses, structural chiralities, and geometric source configurations are completely preserved—even when the underlying Lie algebraic value simplifies to zero. Finally, we bridge this abstract framework to hardware-computable execution by implementing a finite-support infrastructure (Finsupp), dropping evaluation complexity from infinite functional spaces to sparse, live coordinate loops. The resulting hybrid engine provides an infallible framework for optimized, zero-information-loss computing across arbitrary geometric dimensions (d=256). As a formally verified Lean 4 compiler architecture for multi-dimensional geometric lattices, it eliminates history loss during algebraic simplification. While standard numeric compilers erase data lineage when expressions evaluate or cancel out, this engine preserves full structural provenance by enforcing a rigid topological homeomorphism between syntactic expression trees and physical execution states. By transitioning from abstract maps to finite-support functions (Finsupp), we achieve live runtime capability on sparse coordinate grids. The resulting hybrid framework guarantees exact origin and metadata recovery at zero runtime performance cost, serving as a blueprint for infallible, fully trust certified, computational physics pipelines.

title: Linguistic Recovery Record Sufficiency: A Preliminary Study Of Feasible Intervention Selection
abstract: A historical record can preserve credible evidence of a linguistic practice while leaving its users unable to choose a feasible recovery intervention. This preliminary study examines the distinctions required for that choice. It separates retained data, interpreted access, available operations, specified recovery targets and the authority to act. Within a Generative Relational architecture, compatible history-bearing configurations can share a record while admitting different successful continuations. A finite characterization requires a common successful policy on each accessible record class. The analysis distinguishes this requirement from reconstructing a complete history and from an already established factorization criterion for a prescribed rule. Examples show that pairwise policy compatibility can fail collectively and that adequate records need not possess a unique coarsest partition. An explicit finite-horizon inquiry model includes observation costs and changed operation domains. A nonlinear activity-support field then supplies an analytically tractable family of regional recovery choices: aggregate and regional records permit different intervention budgets, while sufficiently delayed observation can leave the standardized recovery route unavailable. Observable subalgebras and partial history operators expose the distinction between a record-dependent choice and an executable procedure. Primary documentation and reuse research constrains the linguistic interpretation. The resulting contribution is a scoped integration and worked investigation, with the empirical identification of support, interpretive access, acceptable recovery aims and public authority left as substantive obligations.

title: A anatomia matemática de uma rede neural
abstract: Apresentamos uma introdução matemática às redes neurais artificiais a partir de um problema simples de classificação. Uma reta classificadora conduz naturalmente ao conceito de neurônio artificial; em seguida, discutimos pesos, vieses, funções de ativação e a composição de neurônios em uma pequena rede. O treinamento é introduzido por meio de funções de perda, derivadas, descida do gradiente e retropropagação. Por fim, implementamos o modelo em Python, tornando explícita a correspondência entre as equações e o algoritmo. O objetivo é mostrar como conceitos de Geometria Analítica, Álgebra Linear e Cálculo fornecem uma base acessível para compreender os princípios fundamentais das redes neurais.

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Comprehensive Tutorial Review
authors: Tarana H. Aliyeva Gulnara A. Safarova
abstract: As artificial intelligence transitions into mission-critical and highly regulated domains, the limitations of monolithic, scale-driven deep learning models-particularly regarding computational unsustainability, brittle robustness, and a lack of logical explainability-have become increasingly apparent.This review provides a comprehensive tutorial overview of the convergence of neural, symbolic, and probabilistic paradigms, culminating in the emerging fields of Neuro-Symbolic and Compositional AI.We systematically trace the historical evolution of artificial intelligence, analyze the mathematical and conceptual foundations of its core paradigms, and evaluate state-of-the-art hybrid architectures, such as Logic Tensor Networks, DeepProbLog, and adaptive large language model (LLM)-symbolic solver pipelines.Furthermore, this review addresses the profound system-level implications and computational bottlenecks of these hybrid workloads on modern classical hardware, discussing critical optimizations for edge deployment and emerging synergies with quantum-classical acceleration.Finally, we highlight transformative real-world applications in healthcare, supply chain management, and autonomous robotics, while outlining key challenges in Explainable AI (XAI) metric standardization, data scarcity, and ethical governance.Ultimately, this review serves as a structured guide toward building next-generation cognitive systems that seamlessly combine data-driven learning with mathematically verified reasoning.

abstract: 本研究在受控合成有限规则材料中，描述大语言模型受限恢复对证据与明确未知措辞的反应。采用12个来源、5个配对条件（V1、V2a、V2b、V3、V4）、B1/C两种提示以及GLM-5.3和deepseek-flash两家模型，每格一次，共240个逻辑请求。事前固定材料、顺序、参数、评分、缺失处理和运行停止条件，报告三个共同主要描述端点及逐来源配对变化，不设显著性或科学成功门槛。正式F3请求将在本登记实际公开并核实后开始。 版本：launch-v4-f3-first（2026-10-08）。本阶段优先完成F3恢复；GPT-4.1-mini与TRUE支持判定作为后续单独验收的F1对照，当前未验证通过。旧432项实验及其P1–P3的主要地位、阴性结果不变。本研究不构成开放世界隐私保证，也不以本次登记追认后续才确定的F1细节。完整方案、材料与哈希清单见附件。

title: Amplitude mode in Eliashberg superconductors
abstract: In the BCS theory of superconductivity the amplitude (Higgs) mode is degenerate with the pair-breaking threshold: its frequency coincides with 2Δ, so it is an edge singularity rather than a true collective mode. This is why after a sudden weak perturbation at t=0 its oscillations decay algebraically as 1/t. We show that the retardation effects due to the phonon dynamics in the strong-coupling theory lift this degeneracy. The Higgs mode detaches from the pair-breaking edge 2Δ_g, set by the spectral gap, and becomes a sharp subgap excitation. We determine its frequency from the longitudinal pair susceptibility evaluated directly on the real frequency axis, using the Eilenberger equations for Migdal--Eliashberg theory with the Einstein phonon spectrum. The response of the mass renormalization supplies at least two fifths of the displacement, and possibly all of it: with it switched off, the binding falls below the resolution of the calculation. Its consequences, however, are significant because a percent-level shift transfers about a quarter of the spectral weight of the amplitude channel out of the two-quasiparticle continuum into a discrete energy level. What experiment sees is therefore not the displacement itself but its consequence: amplitude oscillations that persist instead of decaying as 1/t.

title: CV-QKD with noisy coherent states and realistic displacement receivers
abstract: Near-optimal binary coherent state discrimination can be achieved by performing a displacement operation followed by photon detection. This displacement serves as a control parameter that can be tuned to optimize a chosen figure of merit, which makes such receivers attractive beyond state discrimination. Here, we turn this discrimination strategy into a complete continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) protocol based on a binary alphabet of noisy coherent states (displaced thermal states) and displacement receivers. We develop a strategy for estimating the channel parameters with the same displacement receiver, since standard quadrature-based methods do not apply. While a key map can be obtained with on/off detection, we demonstrate that reliable parameter estimation requires photon-number-resolving detection with sufficient resolution. Finite detector resolution underestimates the observed noise and constitutes a potential security loophole, which we quantify and show to be mitigable with modest resolution. We analyze the protocol's security against entangling-cloner collective attacks in the asymptotic regime, for both direct and reverse reconciliation, and show that it can generate secret keys even under noisy state preparation and imperfect detection. Interestingly, we find that the displacement that minimizes the discrimination error probability also performs well for key generation, thus providing a useful and analytically tractable tuning strategy for the CV-QKD receiver. We evaluate the protocol's performance over a range of transmittances and noise parameters, showing that the displacement receiver can outperform conventional homodyne detection in experimentally relevant regimes. Together, our results point to displacement receivers as a promising alternative for CV-QKD implementations.

title: Estimate of Γ(H to gg) at O(α_s^7) from Padé approximants with constraints from large-n_f
abstract: In this work we estimate the first unknown QCD correction to the decay of the Higgs boson into gluons, Hto gg, in the heavy-top limit using Padé approximants built to the perturbative series and to its Borel transform. In the process, we also obtain estimates for the first unknown coefficients of the QCD β function, of the QCD decoupling relation, and of the gluonium correlator. We also provide an updated prediction for the first unknown coefficient of Γ(Hto bb). We determine the polynomial dependence of the perturbative coefficients on the number of quark flavors, n_f. We point out that the large-n_f result for Hto gg can be obtained from results for the gluonium correlator already available in the literature. The coefficient of the highest power of n_f is then imposed as a constraint and is also used as a new test to discard unreliable approximants. The method is validated through the postdiction of the last known coefficient of the series. Our model-independent estimate for the yet unknown coefficient of order α_s^7 of Γ(Hto gg) is -312pm 15 (in the mathrm{MS} scheme with μ=m_H, where m_H is the Higgs mass). With our estimate the residual renormalization-scale dependence of Γ(Hto gg) is reduced by a factor of almost 1.5.

title: Latent Watermarks under Generative Editing: A Benchmark and Analysis of Detection Survival
abstract: Ordinary prompt-based editing can cause latent watermark detection to fail without explicitly targeting the watermark. We benchmark eight watermark methods against five editors across four generative backbones, four editing strengths, and five semantic categories, with edit-validity and threshold checks. Separating editing from seven subsequent distortions reveals that editing alone primarily distinguishes Tree-Ring, while added distortions expose a broader spectrum of detection survival. Sequential edits reveal a second hidden difference: score separation can decline while detection rates remain near their ceiling. Across methods, standardized clean score separation ($d'$) organizes composite-survival tiers, whereas spatial overlap adds little to predicting edit-only survival beyond clean detectability. Embedding-strength interventions in two methods link higher clean separation to higher post-edit separation. In HSTR, the margin contrast is positive, while the angular layout contrast at matched clean separation remains unresolved. Together, outcome decomposition and continuous separation expose differences hidden by aggregate TPR. Method tiers are stable under threshold recalibration at the main operating points and alternative composite weights. Clean $d'$ is thus a useful empirical diagnostic within this benchmark, with mixed transfer to unseen methods. Code and supporting artifacts are planned for a separate release.

title: Sample-based quantum simulation of vibrational structure of polyyne chains
abstract: Predicting anharmonic vibrational spectra is a complex computational task, which becomes quickly infeasible as molecular size and the number of vibrational basis functions increase, leading to an exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. Here, we employ a sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) framework to compute anharmonic vibrational energies and spectra. The approach combines quantum state preparation and sampling with configuration recovery, diagonalization of the Hamiltonian projected in a subspace of basis configurations, and calculation of transition-dipole moments to obtain both vibrational energies and infrared spectra. We investigate two approaches for sampling, namely, vib-LUCJ and vib-SqDRIFT and apply the method to study the polyyne molecules C$_2$H$_2$ and C$_4$H$_2$, reaching representations requiring up to 104 qubits. Beyond energies, transition-dipole calculations reveal that infrared intensities and excited-state composition continue to evolve with basis size through anharmonic mixing and intensity redistribution, even when low-energy eigenvalues appear converged. These results show that sample-based quantum subspace methods can capture spectroscopic information in vibrational spaces far beyond the regime of full diagonalization. Moreover, our simulation identify multi-state recovery and scalable projected-space treatment as central challenges for further scaling sample-based approaches.

title: RT-DETR-World: Transferring Rich LLM Semantics to Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Detection
abstract: Open-vocabulary detection (OVD) recognizes categories unseen during training through textual category queries, yet achieving strong generalization with real-time efficiency remains challenging. Beyond vocabulary scaling, zero-shot generalization may benefit from reusable visual--semantic cues learned from seen data, including attributes, actions, states, and contextual relations. Existing real-time OVD methods primarily emphasize vocabulary coverage and efficient region/query--text matching; under strict efficiency constraints, compact detectors may struggle to absorb rich instance semantics and scene context. We propose RT-DETR-World, a compact DETR-style detector that transfers the rich semantics conveyed by descriptions during training while retaining lightweight query--text matching at inference. We construct GroundingCapv2 with three levels of supervision: category names for standard OVD, object descriptions conveying instance-level semantics, and image descriptions conveying object relations and scene context. These descriptions serve only as training-time semantic supervision. To help the compact detector absorb these semantics, we propose Dual-Path Description Alignment (DDA), combining a deployment-consistent MiniLM pathway with a training-only LLM teacher. MiniLM provides query--category supervision and object-description alignment, while offline teacher features supervise matched queries and global visual representations at the object and image levels, respectively. All teacher features are precomputed, and the teacher-side modules are removed after training. evidence.title: RT-DETR-World: Transferring Rich LLM Semantics to Real-Time Open-Vocabulary Detection
evidence.abstract: Open-vocabulary detection (OVD) recognizes categories unseen during training through textual category queries, yet achieving strong generalization with real-time efficiency remains challenging. Beyond vocabulary scaling, zero-shot generalization may benefit from reusable visual--semantic cues learned from seen data, including attributes, actions, states, and contextual relations. Existing real-time OVD methods primarily emphasize vocabulary coverage and efficient region/query--text matching; under strict efficiency constraints, compact detectors may struggle to absorb rich instance semantics and scene context. We propose RT-DETR-World, a compact DETR-style detector that transfers the rich semantics conveyed by descriptions during training while retaining lightweight query--text matching at inference. We construct GroundingCapv2 with three levels of supervision: category names for standard OVD, object descriptions conveying instance-level semantics, and image descriptions conveying object relations and scene context. These descriptions serve only as training-time semantic supervision. To help the compact detector absorb these semantics, we propose Dual-Path Description Alignment (DDA), combining a deployment-consistent MiniLM pathway with a training-only LLM teacher. MiniLM provides query--category supervision and object-description alignment, while offline teacher features supervise matched queries and global visual representations at the object and image levels, respectively. All teacher features are precomputed, and the teacher-side modules are removed after training. We further propose Relation-Aware Negative Relaxation (RNR), which uses teacher-derived semantic similarities to relax related negatives while preserving exact positives. Experiments demonstrate competitive zero-shot accuracy and a favorable accuracy--efficiency trade-off. The code will be released.

title: Self-attention summary networks for subsurface velocity-model building from common-image gathers
abstract: Common-image gathers (CIGs) contain physically meaningful information about velocity-model errors through reflector focusing and residual moveout, but in conventional imaging workflows they are typically used only as diagnostic tools. In this work, we propose a multiscale self-attention summary network that maps high-dimensional 3D CIG volumes into compact conditioning embeddings for probabilistic subsurface velocity inversion. These learned embeddings preserve offset-dependent kinematic structure and spatial coherence while reducing variability caused by background-velocity mismatch. Conditioned on these summary embeddings, a flow-matching model learns a transport from a Gaussian source distribution to the posterior distribution of plausible velocity fields. Numerical experiments show that, compared with direct conditioning on raw CIGs, the proposed summary network improves posterior velocity inference. In particular, the multiscale attention design provides greater robustness to background-model mismatch, yielding more accurate posterior reconstructions and lower predictive uncertainty.

title: Explainable AI to Guide the Design of Interpretable Prediction Models From High-Dimensional Data, Applied to Falls and Related Injuries in Adults Aged 50 Years or Older: Algorithm Development and Validation
abstract: Code for the Exploratory AI Recommender: feature attributions of a random survival forest are turned into recommendations (features to exclude, non-linear terms and pairwise interactions) for a Cox proportional hazards model, which is then evaluated on held-out data. The repository contains the recommendation and evaluation code used for the main (DataLoch) analysis, demonstrations on three open data sets (GBSG2, ACT and peakVO2), additional analyses on those data sets, and simulations of the recommendation rules. The data processing specific to DataLoch is not included.

title: Atribución de autoría en lingüística forense: comparación textual, validación y límites de la inferencia
abstract: El artículo examina la atribución de autoría como una tarea de la lingüística forense en la que la relación entre un texto cuestionado y uno o varios productores posibles se analiza mediante datos comparables, criterios explícitos y procedimientos sujetos a revisión. El objetivo consiste en sistematizar los principios que organizan la pregunta de autoría, la selección de muestras, la estilística forense, la estilometría, los rasgos recurrentes, los n-gramas, los escenarios cerrados y abiertos, la comunicación digital, la autoría compartida, la copia, la asistencia automática, la validación y la formulación pericial. El estudio sigue una revisión documental analítica de la sección dedicada a la atribución de autoría en Fundamentos de la lingüística forense y de las referencias que esa sección incorpora como apoyo teórico. Los resultados indican que la atribución no descansa en una coincidencia aislada ni en una puntuación automática, sino en la relación entre estabilidad intraautoral, capacidad de distinción, comparabilidad de los textos y evaluación de alternativas. También se identifica una diferencia metodológica entre clasificar candidatos conocidos y examinar la hipótesis de un autor externo, diferencia que modifica la interpretación del rendimiento. La escritura breve, la edición, la copia, las herramientas de asistencia y la variación pluricéntrica del español introducen fuentes adicionales de heterogeneidad. La discusión sostiene que la validez pericial depende de un protocolo que documente decisiones, reserve datos para comprobación y comunique el alcance de la conclusión sin confundir semejanza lingüística con identidad jurídica. La atribución de autoría se entiende, por ello, como una inferencia gradual sobre procesos de producción textual y no como una identificación automática de personas.

title: Beyond Outcomes: Toward Process-Aware Software Agents
abstract: Autonomous programming agents are commonly evaluated by whether they solve software tasks, providing limited insight into the execution processes that lead to success or failure. We present a process-centric approach to evaluating agent behavior through trajectories. We introduce Graphectory, which captures the structural organization of agent execution, and Langutory, which abstracts low-level actions into software engineering phases to characterize problem-solving strategies. We further relate observed execution to intended workflows through plan compliance. Across thousands of trajectories, our analysis uncovers behavioral patterns that outcomes alone cannot explain, including persistent inefficiencies in successful runs and substantial variation in how agents translate plans into execution. These findings highlight the importance of understanding how agents execute, laying the foundation for the process-aware optimization of software agents.

title: Mining Tactics for Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: Automated theorem proving is essential for the formal verification of safety-critical systems. As the corpus of formal proofs grows, a natural paradigm is to learn from existing proofs. However, current learning-based approaches predominantly train Large Language Models (LLMs) as end-to-end provers, which yields resource-intensive, opaque systems. Conversely, while traditional symbolic provers are computationally efficient, how to automatically improve these solvers from data remains an open challenge.

title: SUSQA: A sustainability accounting protocol for quantum federated learning
abstract: Quantum machine learning is often described as a path toward more sustainable federated learning: smaller quantum models could, in principle, reduce the network traffic and resource footprint of training medical-imaging models across hospitals without sharing patient data. Today this claim cannot be checked, because published studies report their costs in ways that cannot be compared with one another. This paper introduces SUSQA, a simple accounting protocol that makes such claims testable. Alongside conventional accuracy, SUSQA reports four costs of a training run: the size of the model, the total data communicated between hospitals and the server, the amount of quantum computation consumed, and how well the trained model tolerates hardware noise. The protocol is demonstrated on three public medical-imaging benchmarks, comparing two conventional neural networks with a small hybrid quantum–classical model, and the noise results are checked against a noise model built from the calibration data of a real quantum processor, evaluated in simulation. The energy and carbon footprint of training are also measured with an established tracking tool. The case studies show that no single approach wins everywhere: the hybrid case study matches the conventional networks on one task while communicating a fraction of the data, stabilises training on a second task, and loses accuracy on a third. The value of the protocol is that it makes all of these trade-offs visible in one report. A reference implementation is released as open-source software.

title: Auditing LLM Program Search for Bermudan Stopping with Primal--Dual Certificates
abstract: LLM program-search agents are usually judged by the score that drives their search. We study LLM-driven search over Python exercise policies for Bermudan options, an optimal stopping problem where a trusted evaluator owns the simulation and a dual upper bound~$U$. For any policy, $0 \le V^\star - L_π\le U - L_π$; we report Monte Carlo estimates of both bounds with their sampling error. We audit 24 generation attempts from two pipelines, a six-pair feedback-representation ablation, and a holdout evaluated after selection was frozen. No selected generated program improves on Ridge LSMC consistently or by more than Monte Carlo uncertainty; holdout gap scores lie within $0.002$ of it. On six one-dimensional puts, a high-precision binomial reference places Ridge within Monte Carlo noise of optimal and attributes 99\% of the estimated gap to dual-bound looseness, so this dual audits validity but cannot certify progress at the search's scale. Structured memory showed no benefit over score-only memory in this ablation. Whether search ``worked'' depends on reporting rules: retaining the initial reference, freezing selection before holdout, and counting failures.

title: A Second-Order Asymptotic Expansion for Nonlinear Filtering in the Lorenz--63 System
abstract: A challenge in nonlinear filtering is to incorporate nonlinear effects into approximations of the conditional mean while retaining a finite-dimensional recursive algorithm. We derive a second-order asymptotic expansion of the filtering mean with respect to the system-noise intensity. We apply this expansion to the Lorenz--63 model, a prototypical three-dimensional chaotic dynamical system. The first-order approximation is computed using a Kalman--Bucy filter for the system linearized around the deterministic reference trajectory. The second-order correction incorporates the Hessian of the Lorenz--63 drift and is computed through a closed recursive system with 3+9+18=30 independent scalar components. The full system, including the reference trajectory and the first-order mean and covariance, has 42 independent scalar components. To support stable tracking of chaotic trajectories over long time intervals, we introduce recentering of the expansion and redistribution of Gaussian components between expansion orders. In the numerical experiments, we compare the proposed algorithm with an ensemble transform Kalman filter (ETKF) as a practical benchmark and a particle filter (PF) as a numerical reference. Under the full-observation settings, the proposed algorithm achieves a lower root-mean-square error relative to the truth and a smaller distance to the 10,000-particle PF reference than the 20-member ETKF. These results suggest that the proposed second-order extension of Kalman filtering has the potential to balance filtering accuracy and computational cost.

title: SPLIT-RL: Staged Perception-Language Reasoning Training with Claim-Level Advantages
abstract: Vision-Language (VL) reasoning requires a model to both extract relevant and accurate information from an image (visual reasoning, VR), and to infer the answer from it (language reasoning, LR). Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards typically trains both through a single chain-of-thought with a final-answer reward. This gives every CoT token the same sequence-level advantage, failing to distinguish capability specific errors. We propose SPLIT-RL, a staged post-training approach that trains VR and LR in disjoint phases. Because a group's rollouts differ along one capability at a time, the group-relative advantage isolates it, and each phase is optimized using phase-specific reward. We further introduce Claim-Level Advantage (CLA-GRPO), which decomposes VR-phase rollouts into atomic visual claims and provides a fine-grained advantage at claim level based on visual-type group formation. Although trained in two phases, trained policy is evaluated like GRPO model, with a single CoT call at inference time. Under this protocol, SPLIT-RL improves average accuracy over GRPO by 1.4-6.1 points across Qwen3-VL models from 2B to 30B-A3B and InternVL3.5-8B. Evaluating each capability using an oracle based diagnostic shows that answer-only GRPO leaves perception unchanged, whereas SPLIT-RL improves both VR and LR.

title: Twist Flow for Inverse Problems
abstract: In Bayesian inverse problems, posterior sampling requires generating samples that are consistent with given observations while capturing the range of plausible solutions. Direct conditional generative models introduce latent noise to model this ambiguity, but paired inverse-problem training can still encourage an almost deterministic map from the observation to the target. As a result, generated samples may be observation-consistent while under-representing posterior variability, especially when the posterior is multimodal, leading to undercoverage, mode distortion, or artificial transitions between distinct feasible solutions. We propose joint twist-flow, an augmented flow-matching formulation that learns a continuous transport from the augmented source state $(z_x, y)$ to the augmented terminal state $(x, z_y)$. Here x is the target variable, $y$ is the observation, $z_x$ is the Gaussian reference coordinate for posterior sampling, and $z_y$ is a Gaussian likelihood-side coordinate associated with the observation branch. Under a Gaussian observation model, $z_y$ is motivated by the normalized observation residual associated with observation compatibility. Its role is not to replace uncertainty in $x$, but to couple generated samples of x to observation consistency, helping reduce likelihood-inconsistent variation while preserving variability in weakly constrained directions. We validate the method on low-dimensional inverse problems with reference posterior samples, where joint twist-flow better preserves multimodal posterior support than a direct conditional-flow baseline. We further evaluate the method on image restoration and seismic subsurface velocity-model inversion, showing increased posterior variability while maintaining observation consistency.

We validate the method on low-dimensional inverse problems with reference posterior samples, where joint twist-flow better preserves multimodal posterior support than a direct conditional-flow baseline. We further evaluate the method on image restoration and seismic subsurface velocity-model inversion, showing increased posterior variability while maintaining observation consistency.

title: ReqEvolve: User-Oriented Software Self-Evolution through Automatic Requirement Interpretation
abstract: The paradigm of software self-evolution enables systems to autonomously extend and reconfigure their own capabilities during execution in response to technical specifications. Yet requests for new functionality often originate from end users and are rarely expressed in technical terms. As a result, developers must translate user needs into technical specifications before the system can evolve, delaying early validation of the requested functionality by preventing users from immediately observing the resulting behaviour. To address this gap, we present ReqEvolve, a runtime code generation system that enables user-driven self-evolution by accepting high-level user requests. The system integrates automatic requirements engineering (RE) and test-driven development (TDD) to transform these requests into executable functionality through clarification, specification decomposition, test generation, and runtime integration. We evaluate ReqEvolve on 72 software evolution cases across 18 projects against two baselines: SpecFix, an RE-focused code generation approach, and an ablation variant of our system. ReqEvolve achieves 89.2% Pass@1, outperforming SpecFix by 18.8% (p < 0.01, r = 0.79, large effect) and the ablation baseline by 32.6% (p < 0.001, r = 0.88, large effect). These results provide initial evidence that user-driven self-evolution is a viable paradigm for autonomously extending software capabilities from user requests, thereby accelerating requirements validation prior to developer verification.

title: Wide neural networks: From non-Gaussian random fields at initialization to the NTK geometry of training
abstract: Recent developments in applications of artificial neural networks with over n = 10 14 parameters make it extremely important to study the large n behavior of such networks. Most works studying wide neural networks have focused on the infinite width n → + ∞ limit of such networks and have shown that, at initialization, they correspond to Gaussian processes [12] , [23] . In this work we will study their behavior for large, but finite n . Our main contributions are the following: • The computation of the corrections to Gaussianity in terms of an asymptotic series in n − 1 2 . The coefficients in this expansion are determined by the statistics of parameter initialization and by the activation function. • The quantitative control, in terms of the width n , of the evolution of the outputs of (finite) networks, during training, by computing deviations from the limiting infinite width case (in which the network evolves through a linear flow). This as been the subject of several previous works, notably [2] , [10] , [16] , [21] , [25] ; our results improve previous estimates and along the way also provide sharper decay rates for the (finite width) NTK in terms of n , valid during the entire training procedure. • Estimating how the deviations from Gaussianity evolve with training in terms of n . In particular, using a certain metric in the space of measures we find that, along training, the resulting measure is within n − 1 2 ( log ⁡ n ) + of the time dependent Gaussian process corresponding to the infinite width network (which is explicitly given by precomposing the initial Gaussian process with the linear flow corresponding to training in the infinite width limit).

title: Unrecorded Evaluation Provenance in a Clinical Diagnosis Benchmark: A Forensic Case Study of Scored-Artifact Mismatch
abstract: We report a single, forensically reconstructed incident in which a fixed-case benchmark used to tune a clinical differential-diagnosis system's ranking engine measured the output of an internal, partially-tuned candidate list rather than the list ultimately shown to a clinician, and no field in the system's run-tracking tables recorded which of the two a given benchmark run had actually scored. Reported top-1 accuracy on a 120-case internal suite rose from 35.0% to 55.8% over seven runs during a single tuning session; an independent remeasurement against the deployed decision path approximately ten days later returned 27.5% (displayed as 28%), which at face value suggests the benchmark had been badly inflated. We show that comparison is not supportable as stated: the 27.5% figure mixed two different scoring-engine configurations because of an unrelated, unpinned engine-selection mechanism; isolating each configuration separately gives 25.8% for the older configuration and 37.5% for the newer one, neither of which is a clean substitute for a measurement taken at the time of the session. We reconstruct the incident using version-control history and live application-database queries. Because our first-pass reconstruction itself converged on an overstated causal story under leading investigative prompts, we also conducted a second, deliberately blind and adversarial re-verification pass that narrowed the claim to what the evidence actually supports. We identify three concurrent contributors to the apparent benchmark-to-deployment gap, directly quantify one of them (an engine-selection confound in the available comparator), and show why the available evidence cannot separately estimate the other two's individual contributions. We argue this incident is an instance of a broader class of evaluation-harness failure: evaluation code that silently scores an unintended artifact, with no logged record of which artifact was scored. This particular instance was never reported anywhere and so is invisible to the public-issue-mining methodology used by the largest empirical studies of evaluation-harness defects we are aware of; we treat single-incident forensic reconstructions such as this one as a necessary complement to that methodology, not as evidence about the class's overall prevalence. We discuss implications for evaluation-harness design during rapid, AI-assisted iterative development, and for provenance requirements in clinical decision-support evaluation specifically, where downstream regulatory frameworks already condition non-device status on a system's outputs being independently reviewable.

title: The Geometry of Narrative Reports: An Exploratory Comparison of Recalled, Imagined, Dream, and Machine-Generated Text
abstract: This exploratory working paper accompanies the revised ebook The Imagined Life: Living Inside a Dreaming Brain, by Mayone Maha Rajan (ebook ISBN 9798235084476). Chapter 4 links to this paper for the methods, numeric results, and limitations behind its discussion. Ebook information: The Imagined Life. The audit compares 500 recalled, imagined, dream, and machine-generated reports per group using two sentence encoders. Archived metrics and full-report centroid distances reproduce, but substantial report-length differences and encoder-dependent equal-length checks limit the original explanatory interpretation. The paper does not establish a causal fingerprint of ungrounding, a common brain-machine algorithm, or artificial experience. The release provides numeric tables, source-row mappings without worker identifiers, and analysis code. It does not redistribute raw human narratives or sentence embeddings, and does not independently reconstruct the embedding stage. AI assisted code and drafting; the author reviews and takes responsibility for the release. This is a working paper, not peer reviewed.

title: Snapshot of Fiddle Tool Repository
abstract: ==== FIDDLE ARCHIVAL VERSION ====This is an archival version of the "Fiddle" tool written about in the ATC 2026short paper "Cold-Patching for Faster Edit-Compile-Run Cycles" (in fact, thisversion has been slightly improved since the experiments in that paper, e.g.,replacing the C++ patchelf tool with a slimmed down version in C). It is not intended to be a particularly good version, just a snapshot storedon Zenodo with a DOI so it remains perpetually available. ==== THIS IS PROBABLY NOT WHAT YOU'RE LOOKING FOR! ====I actively use Fiddle, and maintain the latest version which you can learnabout and download from the homepage at: https://lair.masot.net/fiddle ==== IF THIS IS WHAT YOU'RE LOOKING FOR ... ====In the off chance you are just interested in "what happened for the ATC paper",let me give you a quick tour. First, notice that Fiddle is written in a dialect of C called MaC. There isa complete copy of MaC bundled here in the vendored-mac subdirectory, andrunning "make" here will build MaC before using MaC to build Fiddle. Second, notice that the focus of the ATC paper was on the use of Fiddle asa cold-patching tool to replace linkers (in some scenarios). The code for thatlives almost entirely in the directory src/patch. You can ignore thedirectories src/pyc and src/package, which are more "flavorful" layers on topof src/patch. Within src/patch, you will find the files: - src/patch/runtime_patcher.c: this contains the constructor that actually gets executed when you run a patched executable, i.e., the code to overwrite functions and objects to point to the 'patched' versions. - src/patch/rewrite_elf.c: this is a slimmed-down version of patchelf, which does things like "dynamize" symbols (copy them from the .symtab to the .dynsym) and add libraries as DT_NEEDED entries in the .dynamic section. - src/patch/elf.c: does some "read-only" things with ELF files, e.g., extracting the symbols from the file's symbol tables. - src/patch/cmd_patch.c: actually performs/orchestrates the patching process. Some things are better commented in src/main.c than in their own files. ==== EXPERIMENTS ====The directory design/experiments contains a number of experiments performedthroughout the course of developing Fiddle. MOST OF THESE ARE IRRELEVANTTODAY. The ones that are relevant to the paper are: - design/experiments/atc_26: measure compilation and patching time for four large projects. - design/experiments/microbenchmark_atc_26: microbenchmarks for the startup and runtime overhead of patched vs. unpatched executables. - design/experiments/vim_benchmark_atc_26: a more "real world" running time overhead evaluation using vim. - design/experiments/detecting_lto: confirm that Fiddle properly detects and errors out when given an object file compiled with LTO.

title: Distributionally-robust heterogeneous graph neural networks via relation-aware grouping
abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains a key challenge for heterogeneous graph neural networks (HGNNs), which often exhibit substantial performance degradation under real-world distribution shifts. While Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) has proven effective in promoting OOD generalization in various domains, its application to heterogeneous graphs remains largely unexplored. This gap stems from a fundamental obstacle: the complex, multi-relational nature of heterogeneous graphs renders conventional group definitions, which rely on explicit node attributes, inadequate. To bridge this gap, we propose DroHGNN, a GroupDRO-based framework for OOD generalization on heterogeneous graphs. DroHGNN introduces a relation-aware soft grouping mechanism coupled with a two-stage optimization procedure to enhance OOD robustness. Specifically, DroHGNN learns soft group assignments through learnable prototypes over relation-specific node representations. These assignments serve as optimization-oriented group proxies for GroupDRO, which minimizes worst-case group risk. To encourage structural coherence of the inferred assignments, we further introduce a heterogeneous graph structural consistency constraint that regularizes the group assignments of structurally connected target nodes. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world benchmarks show that DroHGNN consistently achieves strong OOD performance compared with competitive baselines. Notably, under degree-distribution shifts on the ArXiv dataset, DroHGNN outperforms NaiveDRO and the leading baseline CaNet by 23.3% and 6.5% in Macro-F1, respectively. Moreover, relative gains of up to 3.2% in average Macro-F1 under the inductive temporal setting further demonstrate its effectiveness under heterogeneous distribution shifts.

title: RoBART: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees with Tree-Specific Rotations
abstract: Bayesian additive regression trees (BART) can require many splits to approximate boundaries misaligned with the predictor axes. RoBART assigns each tree a rotation shared by all internal nodes, retaining axis-aligned splits in rotated coordinates and constant leaves. We jointly propose a Givens rotation sequence and cutpoints on the resulting grid by Metropolis-Hastings and establish reversibility with respect to the conditional posterior with leaf means integrated out. For additive functions with component-specific rotations and anisotropic Hölder smoothness, we prove posterior contraction in empirical $L_2$ distance and for the noise standard deviation. Under the stated prior, design, and grid conditions, with fixed numbers of predictors, trees, and components and no more components than trees, the rate is a sum of componentwise rates determined by smoothness and the number of rotated coordinates used. We also establish a posterior contraction lower bound showing that there exist functions for which RoBART adapts to the intrinsic dimension but axis-aligned BART does not.

title: Smooth spectral statistics of random perturbations of Schrödinger operators near Anosov energy levels
abstract: We investigate the spectral statistics of random perturbations of semiclassical Schrödinger operators on compact manifolds, near energy levels corresponding to chaotic classical dynamics. The prototypical example is that of an operator h^2Δ+V(x) that is perturbed by a smooth potential h^αV_ω with αin (0,1), and V_ω is a random potential that decorrelates on distances h^β, with 0<β<2α. We show that for a generic perturbation, the spectral fluctuations of the smoothed counting function of eigenvalues obey a universal behavior at a certain mesoscopic scale, which is coherent with the predictions of random matrix theory.

title: The generalized lower triangular process prior
abstract: In the analysis of multivariate data, factor models represent a powerful technique for both reducing dimensionality and facilitating qualitative understanding of the latent determinants governing the observed data. Interpretability, however, is often hindered by the non-identifiability of factor loading matrices due to rotational invariance. A prevailing strategy to address this issue is to consider positive lower triangular structures. A relaxation of the latter condition has been recently proposed in the literature with the so called generalized lower triangular structure. However, its Bayesian implementation presents substantial challenges, requiring complex reversible-jump algorithms and making prior elicitation difficult because of the limited interpretability of the model parameters. In this paper, we introduce a generalized lower triangular process prior that allows both global and within-component sparsity structures for learning both the number of factors and possible sparsity structures within the vector of observations. The proposed approach provides straightforward prior parameters elicitation exploiting possibly different prior information on the rank and sparsity characteristics. We also explore connections with the Indian buffet process, providing further insight into the sparsity structure induced by the proposed prior. Posterior computation can be performed resorting to a Gibbs sampler with Metropolis-Hastings moves. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through comprehensive simulations and the analysis of the Big Five Personality Test data.

title: What Makes Synthetic Hard Negatives Work in Vision-Language Pretraining?
abstract: Synthetic hard negatives generated in the representation space have proven effective for unimodal self-supervised learning, but transferring this idea to vision-language pretraining is not straightforward. We analyze six representation-space synthesis strategies and identify two failure modes in their transfer to vision-language pretraining: cross-modal constructions that produce overly easy negatives or pull them toward the query, and intra-modal constructions that incorporate the matched positive. We also observe logit-scale saturation when training with synthetic hard negatives and a learnable temperature, and find that fixing the temperature improves downstream performance. Using this geometric analysis we propose SNAP, which generates intra-modal hard negatives that never involve the positive from either modality, avoiding both failure modes entirely. SNAP is model-agnostic, requires no external generative models, and adds less than 10% training time overhead. Evaluated on top of CLIP and FLIP across multiple architectures and datasets, SNAP delivers consistent improvements on zero-shot retrieval, zero-shot classification, and linear probe evaluation.

title: Ream: Unfolding Mutual Awareness in Human-Agent Workspaces
abstract: As AI agents work alongside humans in shared workspaces, a mutual awareness challenge arises: agents act at speeds that outpace human monitoring, and users' evolving interests are not always expressed in chat. This challenge is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers. We present Ream, a literature review workspace that supports mutual awareness through structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within these documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. In studies with eighteen researchers, participants used these traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work. These findings inform how engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

evidence.title: Ream: Unfolding Mutual Awareness in Human-Agent Workspaces
evidence.abstract: As AI agents work alongside humans in shared workspaces, a mutual awareness challenge arises: agents act at speeds that outpace human monitoring, and users' evolving interests are not always expressed in chat. This challenge is especially pressing in literature review, where both parties retrieve, read, and synthesize a growing body of papers. We present Ream, a literature review workspace that supports mutual awareness through structured artifacts, bidirectional engagement tracking, and localized visualizations. Users can see each party's activity within these documents, and agents can retrieve the same history to guide their work. In studies with eighteen researchers, participants used these traces to inspect evidence, steer agents, communicate through annotations, and reflect on their research focus. Shared histories also helped agents build on earlier work. These findings inform how engagement traces within shared documents can support transparency, personalized assistance, and coordination in human-agent knowledge work.

title: Shortcuts for adiabatic and variational algorithms in molecular simulation
abstract: Quantum algorithms offer a promising route toward computational advantage, but current implementations remain constrained by limited coherence and gate errors, making circuit complexity and noise sensitivity critical considerations. Here, we develop a shortcuts-to-adiabaticity strategy for molecular ground-state preparation and apply it to both digitized adiabatic quantum computing and the variational quantum eigensolver. In the adiabatic framework, we construct an approximate counterdiabatic (CD) Hamiltonian using a nested-commutator expansion. For the molecular systems considered, the CD correction accelerates state preparation and improves energy convergence in the fast-evolution regime, enabling a target accuracy to be reached with a lower implemented-operator count. In the variational setting, we introduce the adiabatic gauge ansatz ($\mbox{AGA}$), obtained by promoting the Pauli-string components generated by the approximate adiabatic gauge potential (AGP) to independent variational generators. We further propose a reduced variant, $\mbox{AGAR}$, that retains only Pauli generators with weight not larger than two, substantially reducing the ansatz size while maintaining competitive accuracy over the regimes considered. Benchmarks on $\mathrm{LiH}$ and $\mathrm{BeH}_2$ show that the proposed ansätze achieve accuracies competitive with established approaches such as UCCSD. Experiments on the \texttt{IBM\_basquecountry} superconducting quantum processor, together with simulations under depolarizing noise, show that the reduced CD-inspired ansatz yields smaller energy discrepancies than UCCSD under the noise conditions considered. Overall, our results demonstrate how AGP-inspired operator structures can be used to balance accuracy and implementation cost in molecular simulations on current noise-limited quantum hardware.

title: Prepoznavanje zgodovinskih imenskih entitet v jezikih z omejenimi viri v dobi velikih jezikovnih modelov
abstract: We present a comparative evaluation of encoder-based and generative approaches for named entity recognition (NER) on historical Slovene parliamentary records. Using a manually annotated subset of the Carniolan Provincial Assembly Corpus Kranjska 1.0, we evaluate a range of locally deployable open-weight models within a unified multishot prompting framework. Our experiments compare traditional supervised encoderbased systems with modern instruction-tuned generative models across both strict and fuzzy evaluation settings. The results show that larger generative models achieve the best overall performance and demonstrate strong multilingual transfer capabilities, while smaller encoder-based systems remain highly competitive in terms of efficiency, inference speed, and person recognition accuracy. However, all models struggle with the extraction of more ambiguous entity types in historical texts, such as locations and organizations.

title: 09_pickle_free_records
abstract: The 09_pickle_free_records folder of the code package provides lossless, pickle-free copies of all 17,622 classified event records. The classified event-level waveform data (npz) directory holds the .npz files in five class folders: blasting (6,512), mechanical_mining (7,690), microseismic (1,401), small_landslide (148), and transport_vehicles (1,871). Each file keeps the stem of its source .npy file and all six field values unchanged, with no filtering, resampling, amplitude scaling, or relabelling. The UTF-8 index records_index.csv lists, for every record, its record ID, class, the relative paths of both files, sensor ID, trigger onset and termination, sampling rate, number of samples, and separate SHA-256 checksums for the .npy and .npz files. The loader load_event.py reads the .npz version by default with allow_pickle=False and checks its checksum, schema, sampling interval, and metadata; its --verify-alloption checks every record. Three accompanying files complete the folder. The script build_npz_release.pyrebuilds the .npz files and the index from the original .npy dataset. The report conversion_report.json documents that all 17,622 records were reopened with allow_pickle=False and passed all 105,732 field comparisons, and records the conversion provenance. README.txt describes the folder contents, record format, path conventions, and usage.

title: Replication package: Are European Statistical APIs Ready for Small Open-Weight LLM Agents? A Matched-Concept Benchmark with Eurostat Interface Interventions
abstract: Replication package for a matched-concept benchmark that tests whether small open-weight large language model (LLM) agents can retrieve exact official figures from European statistical APIs. The same 125 tasks (ten macroeconomic concepts, five operations, three countries) were requested from Eurostat, the World Bank, the European Central Bank and the OECD and answered by four locally served open-weight models (Qwen2.5-Coder 7B and 14B, Llama 3.1 8B, Gemma 2 9B) under three conditions: task only, task plus a structural metadata card, and card plus a retry budget (4,500 task-runs). Two interventions on the 50 Eurostat tasks added an interface note with a working JSON-stat access example (X1) or documentation of an SDMX-CSV endpoint (X2) (1,200 task-runs). The package contains the run notebook with the complete benchmark code and prompts, the frozen gold standard with raw API snapshots, all run records, the archived analysis notebook and the post-hoc analysis pipeline used in the article. Evaluation and analyses are reproducible from the saved records without GPU or API access.

title: Modular Utilities For Numeric And General-purpose Embedding In R
abstract: MUNGE is an open-source R package providing a modular, statistically rigorous pipeline for automated exploratory data analysis (EDA) of tabular data. The package is designed to produce structured, machine-readable statistical fingerprints of mixed-type datasets, bridging classical statistical characterization with downstream embedding and transfer learning workflows. The pipeline operates at two levels of analysis: column-level characterization of individual numeric variables and matrix-level structural analysis of the full data matrix, each paired with human-readable interpretation functions that translate raw descriptors into contextual natural language summaries.

title: A certificateless sanitizable signcryption scheme for air-ground collaborative transportation system
abstract: Air-ground collaborative transportation systems present a promising approach to improving safety and efficiency by facilitating real-time information sharing among UAVs, ground infrastructure, and intelligent vehicles through aerial networks. Yet, the reliance on open wireless networks exposes them to security threats such as eavesdropping, tampering, disruption and message forgery. Signcryption provides an effective cryptographic solution to mitigate these threats. However, existing methods still face challenges in security and efficiency, including: (1) key escrow risk and inefficiency stemming from centralized architectures; (2) active data leakage by malicious data senders. To address these issues, this paper introduces a Certificateless Sanitizable Signcryption scheme (AGC-CSS). In AGC-CSS, the generation of the private key requires contributions from both the user and the KGC. Even if the KGC is breached, the attacker cannot reconstruct the complete private key, which alleviates the risk of key escrow. Meanwhile, our scheme integrates encryption and signature into a single process, ensuring data confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity while maintaining high efficiency. Moreover, we designed a sanitization mechanism in which a sanitizer can re-randomize both the ciphertext and signature to prevent malicious senders. Formal security proofs and performance analyses indicate that the AGC-CSS scheme can resist various common attacks and applies to air-ground collaborative networks.

title: Looking Under the Streetlight: Evaluation in Generative Molecular Dynamics
abstract: This position paper argues that the generative molecular dynamics (GenMD) community is not properly evaluating its progress: current evaluations let a model match what is reported while being arbitrarily wrong on what was claimed, which risks over-claiming advantage over classical baselines. This reflects a structural misalignment between common evaluation practices and the scientific tasks the field sets for itself. The reason is that the ground truth---exhaustive molecular dynamics on the systems of interest---is computationally costly, and this cost is what motivates the field. With ground truth inaccessible, evaluation drifts toward convenient proxies, and the resulting norms entrench easily. We identify misaligned evaluation patterns that persist as a community-level equilibrium, and propose concrete observables, reporting standards, and benchmark designs, both computational and experimental, that better reflect what GenMD aspires to deliver. Our aim is to give the field shared language and tools for evaluation that match its scientific ambitions before today's conventions calcify into norms.

title: Edge Accuracy Is Not Enough: Why Dynamics-Learned Structure Fails to Transfer to Inverse Problems
abstract: A natural strategy for inverse problems with scarce labelled data is to transfer relational structure learned from abundant forward-simulation data. We show this strategy fails systematically, even when it satisfies the standard theoretical justification for why structure should help. We prove that approximate structure provides estimation-error benefits whenever the edge error satisfies $Δ< n^2 - kn$, reducing sample complexity from $O(n^2)$ to $O(kn+Δ)$. Structure learned via Neural Relational Inference (NRI) from dynamics prediction satisfies this condition, yet on a source-localisation task across 180 CFD-simulated hydrogen-leak scenarios and 180 acoustic scenarios, it degrades performance by 116% and 201% relative to a flexible, task-optimised attention baseline, while a physics-based prior (Green's function) degrades by only 69-72%. Four independent lines of evidence show this is not a tuning failure: NRI improves only 0.5% when given 18x more training data (versus 16.6% for the task-optimised baseline, $p<0.001$); performance is insensitive to the NRI edge threshold across a wide range; the dynamics-learned graph overlaps the task-optimal graph on only 6% of edges; and two further dynamics-derived structure estimators (correlation- and mutual-information-based) show no measurable benefit over a structure-free baseline, with the correlation-based estimator performing markedly worse. We formalise this gap as a statement about approximation error that the edge-accuracy condition cannot control, and we provide a lightweight transferability test (Jaccard similarity against a partially-observed target-task graph) that separates successful from failed transfer in all four domain/structure pairs we evaluate, using under an hour of computation and 15-20% of target-domain data; we present this as a heuristic calibrated on few cases, not a validated general threshold.

title: Toward Part-Aware Choral Transcription with singing voice assignment
abstract: Single-instrument automatic music transcription (AMT) has advanced substantially, yet choral applications require soprano, alto, tenor, and bass (SATB) to be transcribed as separate parts. Recent note-level choral AMT instead produces a single merged note track, limiting rehearsal, education, and score reconstruction. To address this limitation, we introduce Part-aware Choral Transcription (PawCT), to our knowledge the first end-to-end neural framework that identifies active SATB parts from choral audio and transcribes each into a separate note-level track. PawCT combines part-specific onset, offset, and frame prediction with part-presence estimation, union-level supervision, and structured training targets using a range prior (RP) based on SATB pitch ranges and its ordered-continuity (OC) extension, which adds within-part melodic continuity and cross-part pitch ordering. On YouChorale, PawCT-RP-OC achieves a macro part-aware note F1 of 0.225 at a 50-ms onset tolerance, outperforming an adapted choral baseline (0.165) by 36.4% relative and a two-stage post-hoc assignment pipeline (0.175). Its part-agnostic variant, PagCT, achieves a 50-ms onset F1 of 0.382, compared with 0.237 for the previous state-of-the-art choral AMT model. Cross-dataset evaluations on CSD and Cantoria further assess performance under dataset shift. These results demonstrate the benefit of jointly modeling note transcription and vocal-part assignment. Code and demos are available at https://hanyu-meng.github.io/Paw_Choral_AMT_Demo/.

title: CATune: Structural Constraint-Aware Bayesian Optimization for DBMS Configuration Tuning
abstract: Modern DBMSs expose hundreds of configuration knobs, resulting in a high-dimensional and heterogeneous search space that makes automated tuning costly. Existing ML-based tuning systems typically treat the configuration domain as box-constrained and rely on workload feedback to implicitly capture inter-knob relationships. However, DBMS documentation specifies deterministic knob dependency constraints, particularly ordering constraints, that characterize structurally valid regions of the configuration space. We present CATune, a constraint-aware Bayesian optimization (BO) framework that models deterministic inter-knob ordering constraints as structural components of the search domain. Instead of learning feasibility boundaries through sampled violations, CATune performs optimization within a constraint-consistent subspace. We develop a topology-aware sampling strategy that respects dependency structure during exploration and avoids the inefficiencies of post-hoc constraint handling. To enable automated constraint discovery, we further design a precision-first extraction pipeline that combines LLM-based parsing with reliability safeguards to mitigate hallucinated dependencies. Experiments on PostgreSQL and MySQL using TPC-C and TPC-H workloads show that CATune substantially improves both sample efficiency and final tuning quality across surrogate models and BO frameworks. Under default ranges, CATune reaches the baseline optimum up to 12.5x faster and improves throughput by up to 63.37%. The improvements persist under knowledge-guided reduced ranges and alternative optimization implementations. These results demonstrate that explicitly modeling system-defined deterministic ordering constraints enhances optimization robustness and system stability.

title: FUSED-Net: Detecting traffic signs with limited data
abstract: Automatic Traffic Sign Recognition is paramount in modern transportation systems. However, curating large-scale datasets for diverse traffic sign detection remains impractical. In this context, we present FUSED-Net, a novel approach that enhances Few-Shot Object Detection (FSOD) for traffic signs using limited data. FUSED-Net integrates Faster RCNN with Unfrozen Parameters, Pseudo-Support Sets, Embedding Normalization, and Domain Adaptation to improve detection accuracy. Unlike conventional methods, FUSED-Net keeps all parameters unfrozen during training, enabling it to learn effectively from limited samples. A Pseudo-Support Set is generated through data augmentation, enhancing performance by compensating for the scarcity of target domain data. Embedding Normalization reduces intra-class variance, standardizing feature representations. Domain Adaptation, achieved by pre-training on a diverse traffic sign dataset, improves model generalization. Experimental results on the BDTSD dataset demonstrate that FUSED-Net achieves 2.4×, 2.2×, 1.5×, and 1.3× improvements in mAP under 1-shot, 3-shot, 5-shot, and 10-shot scenarios, respectively, compared to state-of-the-art FSOD models. Additionally, FUSED-Net achieves superior performance on the cross-domain FSOD benchmark across multiple settings. The source code and the URLs to download the datasets are available at https://github.com/180041123-Atiq/FUSED-Net.

title: IA nas finanças
abstract: IA nas finanças apresenta um percurso de aplicação de inteligência artificial para gestores financeiros, analistas e consultores.O objetivo do livro é ajudar o leitor a ganhar previsibilidade de caixa e melhorar a qualidade das decisões sobre cobrança, custos e capital de giro. O conteúdo usa casos didáticos fictícios, exemplos e propostas de trabalho para discutir decisões, organização de informações e revisão humana.Ao longo dos 10 capítulos, você encontrará:Fundamentos de IA para equipes financeirasPreparação de planilhas e qualidade dos dadosFluxo de caixa: organização e análise de desviosOrçamento e projeções com premissas explícitasAnálise de custos, margens e rentabilidadeO percurso avança até Projeto prático: um relatório gerencial mensal assistido. As atividades devem ser adaptadas ao contexto e conferidas pelo leitor; os casos fictícios não representam resultados comprovados. Edição digital em EPUB. title: The Admitted Shortcut: Tree search over sub-specifications of a decidable logic — shortcuts under a decided, bound admission record, controlled change of the tables they read, and a forward shortcut with a decided margin, with Tau Chess as the worked example
abstract: A search program saves work by shortcuts that stop a loop over candidates, or skip a candidate, where the choice cannot change. In the method described here the work of a search is spread over small sub-specifications of a logic with a decision procedure, and a shortcut acts only if a statement about its executed text, decided for all assignments of its inputs, is bound to that text by its hash in an admission record; otherwise the condition that reads it has no effect, and the loop runs on without the shortcut (the fallback rule). For shortcuts that only save work, a missing or unfitting admission costs evaluations, not the choice. The same record governs the change of a table a shortcut reads, taken over only when the shortcut's precondition is decided for the new text, and a forward shortcut whose margin is decided over the executed scoring. Around this core the paper describes the exchange of an executed text for a reformulated one of decided equality, the binding of records to the build of the evaluation unit, a search of fixed depth from a number, a depth chosen per phase by a sub-specification, and workers whose merge and shared bound are outputs of an admitted sub-specification. The worked example is Tau Chess, built from sub-specifications of the Tau language, created by Ohad Asor and developed by IDNI AG. Run on builds of its evaluation unit are the search with admission records, a start check that refuses and names the reason, a fallback with the same moves at more calls, the exchange of 19 executed texts, a search of fixed depth with workers call for call equal to a reference model, a game with depth per phase ending in mate, the reopening of an execution unit after an unexpected end, and a learning cycle in which a table proposed from the program's own games is taken over only after the precondition of the reading shortcuts is decided over its text. The forward shortcut exists in a smallest form only. One game against a language model and series of games against a chess program are reported; nothing here is a statement about playing strength. ---

title: Cross-Lingual Real-Time Speech Interaction for Embodied Intelligence: Architecture, Challenges, and Prospects
abstract: Embodied intelligence is rapidly evolving toward natural human-machine interaction, where real-time cross-lingual speech processing is essential for robots to understand and execute commands across languages. This study reviews research progress from January 2010 to November 1, 2025, using CiteSpace to analyze knowledge structure, hotspots, and trends. The year 2010 was selected as the start date because it marks the early emergence of foundational theoretical discussions on embodied intelligence internationally, providing a comprehensive baseline to observe the entire evolutionary trajectory of the field, even though substantive domestic research emerged later around 2015. Results show a sharp rise in research interest after 2023, driven by multilingual interaction and robotics applications. Current hotspots include multimodal representation learning, low-latency speech-to-text models, cross-lingual semantic alignment, and embodied control. The field has progressed through three stages: conceptual foundations, real-time neural integration, and large-model-driven general embodiment. We summarize the technical framework spanning speech recognition, semantic grounding, and action execution, and identify challenges such as latency reduction, noise robustness, and cross-lingual knowledge transfer. Future work should focus on unified speech-action representation, scalable low-latency architectures, adaptive learning, and ethical governance. This study outlines development trends and prospects for cross-lingual real-time speech interaction in embodied intelligence.
